scenes.title: Antilochus Brings the News
scenes.summary: Achilles, by the ships, sees the Achaeans driven back across the plain and fears what his mother once told him: that the best of the Myrmidons would leave the light of the sun while he still lived. Antilochus comes in tears with the grievous news that Patroclus lies dead and that Hector has his armor. Achilles pours dust over his head, fouls his face and his fragrant tunic, and lies great over a great space in the dust, tearing his hair; the slave women he and Patroclus had taken cry aloud and beat their breasts, and Antilochus holds his hands, fearing that he will cut his throat.

scenes.title: Thetis and the Nereids
scenes.summary: Thetis hears her son's cry in the depths of the sea and wails, and all the Nereids gather around her in the silver-white cave; the poet names thirty-three of them. Thetis leads the lament: she bore the best of heroes and reared him like a plant on the slope of an orchard, but she will never welcome him home, and while he lives he grieves and she cannot help him. She goes up out of the sea with her sisters, and they come ashore where the Myrmidons' ships are drawn up around Achilles.

scenes.title: Thetis Comes to Achilles
scenes.summary: Thetis takes her son's head in her hands and asks why he weeps, since Zeus has done what he prayed for. Achilles answers that he has lost Patroclus and his armor, and wishes she had never married a mortal; he will not live unless Hector dies under his spear. Thetis tells him that his own death is ready straight after Hector's, and he accepts it: let him die, since he failed his friend; let strife and anger perish from gods and men; he will win fame and take his death when Zeus wills it. Thetis bids him not go into battle until she brings new armor from Hephaestus at dawn, sends the Nereids back to their father's house, and goes to Olympus.

scenes.title: Iris Sent by Hera
scenes.summary: The Achaeans flee to the ships, and Hector, like a flame, three times seizes the body of Patroclus by the feet, while the two Ajaxes three times thrust him back; he would have dragged it off and won untold glory. Hera sends Iris, without the knowledge of Zeus, to bid Achilles arm: Hector means to cut off the head and fix it on the stakes. Achilles has no armor and his mother has forbidden him to arm; Iris tells him to go to the ditch just as he is and show himself to the Trojans.

scenes.title: The Shout from the Ditch
scenes.summary: Athena throws the aegis around Achilles' shoulders and crowns his head with a golden cloud that blazes like the beacon fires of a besieged island city. He stands at the ditch, apart from the Achaeans, and shouts, and Athena shouts with him; three times his voice rings out like a trumpet, three times the Trojans and their allies are thrown into confusion, and twelve of their best men die among their own chariots and spears. The Achaeans draw Patroclus out of the missiles and lay him on a bier, and Achilles follows, weeping for the friend he sent out with horses and chariot. Hera sends the unwilling sun down to the streams of Oceanus, and the battle ends.

scenes.title: The Trojan Assembly
scenes.summary: The Trojans hold an assembly standing, before supper, trembling because Achilles has appeared. Polydamas, born on the same night as Hector, who alone sees before and after, counsels them to go back into the city at once: Achilles will not stay on the plain, and if he finds them there at dawn, dogs and vultures will eat many Trojans; behind the walls they are safe. Hector rejects him angrily: the Trojans have been penned in long enough, and Troy's treasures sold away; they will take supper by companies, keep watch, and at dawn fight at the ships, and he will face Achilles himself, for Enyalius is impartial. The Trojans applaud him, fools, for Athena has taken away their wits.

scenes.title: The Mourning for Patroclus
scenes.summary: All night the Achaeans mourn Patroclus. Achilles leads the lament, his man-slaying hands on his friend's breast, groaning like a lion whose cubs a deer hunter has snatched away. He tells the Myrmidons that he promised Menoetius to bring his son home to Opus, but both of them are fated to redden the earth at Troy; he will not bury Patroclus until he brings Hector's armor and head, and he will cut the throats of twelve Trojan children at the pyre. They wash the body, anoint it, fill the wounds with ointment, and lay it on a bier under a soft linen cloth and a white cloak.

scenes.title: Zeus and Hera
scenes.summary: Zeus tells Hera that she has had her way in rousing Achilles, as if the Achaeans were her own children. Hera answers that even a mortal accomplishes his purpose against another; how should she, the best of goddesses by birth and as his wife, not stitch together evil for the Trojans in her resentment?

scenes.title: Thetis in the House of Hephaestus
scenes.summary: Thetis comes to the bronze house of Hephaestus and finds him sweating at his bellows, making twenty tripods on golden wheels that can go of themselves into the divine assembly. Charis, his wife, welcomes her and calls him. Hephaestus remembers that Thetis and Eurynome took him in when he had fallen far by the will of his mother, who wanted to hide him away because he was lame, and that he worked for them for nine years in a cave by the stream of Oceanus; he puts away his tools, washes, and comes out, supported by golden handmaids that have mind and voice. Thetis tells her sorrows: married against her will to a mortal, she bore a son who will never come home; his prize was taken from him, his friend killed, his armor lost. Hephaestus promises armor that men will marvel at, wishing he could as surely hide her son from death.

scenes.title: Hephaestus at His Forge
scenes.summary: Hephaestus sets his twenty bellows to work, casts bronze, tin, gold and silver into the fire, and takes up the anvil, hammer and tongs. First he makes a great shield of five layers, with a threefold rim and a silver strap, and on it many intricate designs.

scenes.title: The Earth, the Sky and the Sea
scenes.summary: On the shield he sets the earth, the sky and the sea, the tireless sun and the full moon, and all the constellations: the Pleiades, the Hyades, Orion, and the Bear, also called the Wagon, which alone never bathes in Oceanus.

scenes.title: The City at Peace
scenes.summary: In one of two cities there are weddings and banquets: brides are led through the streets by torchlight to the bridal song, young men dance to flutes and lyres, and the women watch from their doorways. In the place of assembly two men quarrel over the penalty for a man who has perished, one vowing to pay it all, the other refusing to take anything; the people cheer both sides, and the elders, seated on polished stones in the sacred circle, spring up in turn with the heralds' scepters to give judgment, with two talents of gold for the straightest.

scenes.title: The City at War
scenes.summary: Two armies besiege the other city, divided whether to sack it or take half its wealth. The defenders leave their wives, children and old men on the wall and go out to an ambush led by Ares and Pallas Athena, golden and taller than the men. At a river where the herds come to drink they lie in wait, fall on the cattle and sheep, and kill the herdsmen; the besiegers ride to the din, and the two sides fight beside the river, while Strife, Tumult and deadly Doom move among them, dragging the dead and wounded by the feet.

scenes.title: Plowing, Harvest and Vintage
scenes.summary: On a broad fallow field plowmen turn their teams and drink honey-sweet wine at the end of each furrow, and the gold grows dark behind them like plowed earth. On a king's domain hired laborers reap, binders tie the sheaves, and boys carry the handfuls, while the king stands by in silence, glad at heart, and heralds prepare a feast under an oak. In a golden vineyard heavy with black grapes, girls and young men carry the grapes in baskets while a boy plays the lyre and sings the Linus song, and the rest dance after him.

scenes.title: The Herds and the Pastures
scenes.summary: Golden and tin cattle hurry lowing to pasture beside a river, with four golden herdsmen and nine dogs; two lions seize a bull from the front of the herd and devour it, and the dogs only bark at them from a distance. There is a great pasture for white sheep in a lovely glen, with farmsteads, roofed huts and pens.

scenes.title: The Dance
scenes.summary: Hephaestus makes a dancing floor like the one Daedalus made for Ariadne in Cnossus. Young men and maidens dance holding hands at the wrist, the girls in fine linen and garlands, the young men in tunics shining softly with oil, with golden knives on silver straps; they run as easily as a potter's wheel turns, and then in ranks toward each other, while a great throng watches, a singer plays the lyre and two tumblers whirl among them. Around the outermost rim of the shield runs the great river Oceanus.

scenes.title: The Armor Completed
scenes.summary: Hephaestus makes a corselet brighter than fire, a heavy helmet with a golden crest, and greaves of soft tin, and sets the armor before Thetis, who leaps down from snowy Olympus like a hawk, carrying it to her son.

days.label: Day 26
days.note: The third day of battle ends. The Trojans drive the Achaeans to the ships and the Hellespont (18.148–150) until Achilles' shout from the ditch; Hera sends the unwilling sun down to the streams of Oceanus (18.239–242).

days.label: Night of Day 26
days.note: The night after the third day of battle: the Trojans' assembly on the plain, the Achaeans' mourning for Patroclus all night long (18.314–315, 18.354–355), and Thetis' visit to Hephaestus, who makes the armor. Thetis promised to return at dawn with the rising sun (18.136); Day 27 dawns at 19.1.
